gloss: the Arctic Circle; the Arctic region

definitions.gloss: the Arctic Circle; the imaginary line of latitude at about 66°33′ north, marking the southern limit of the area where the sun does not set on at least one day a year
definitions.explanation: Refers to the parallel of latitude that defines the boundary of the Arctic. North of this line, there is at least one day per year on which the sun does not set (the midnight sun) and at least one on which it does not rise (polar night). The same word is also used loosely to mean the entire region inside that line — the high-latitude lands and seas of the far north, including parts of Russia, Canada, the United States (Alaska), Greenland, Iceland, and the Scandinavian countries.

notes:
Composed of ⟦{北極|ほっきょく}→北極：16689_hokkyoku⟧ ('the North Pole; the Arctic') + ⟦{圏|けん}→圏：21183_ken⟧ ('sphere, region, zone'). The suffix ⟦{圏|けん}→圏：21183_ken⟧ forms a productive set of geographic and conceptual zone terms: ⟦{首都圏|しゅとけん}→首都圏：18485_shutoken⟧ ('the Tokyo metropolitan area'), ⟦{成層圏|せいそうけん}→成層圏：05245_seisouken⟧ ('the stratosphere'), ⟦{勢力圏|せいりょくけん}→勢力圏：21934_seiryokuken⟧ ('sphere of influence').

USAGE:
In strict geographical use, {北極圏|ほっきょくけん} denotes the latitude line at about 66°33′N — the formal boundary of the Arctic. In journalistic and everyday use it usually refers more broadly to the Arctic region as a whole, including the lands and seas inside that line.

It is the standard word in Japanese news coverage of climate change, polar exploration, and the indigenous peoples of the far north.
The Arctic Circle is a topic of growing strategic and environmental importance in Japanese news. Articles on Arctic shipping routes ({北極海航路|ほっきょっかいこうろ}), polar bears, indigenous peoples, and climate change frequently use this term.

- ⟦{寒帯|かんたい}→寒帯：04124_kantai⟧: frigid zone — one of the traditional climatic zones of the earth, roughly corresponding to the polar areas.
